title: But What About Social-Emotional Learning?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a reader question about how classroom teachers should handle social-emotional learning when students arrive with disparate outside support, Stuart argues for a two-part answer. First, classroom teachers should cultivate genuine love for students and let SEL growth happen as a byproduct of a loving, mastery-focused classroom rather than as a separate curriculum -- he frames this as a mirror image of Mr. Rogers, where the subject is English or science but the coincidental lesson is about being human. Second, he argues that broader SEL capacity-building for a school community belongs to teams outside the classroom, who should build a habit-forming library of short, consistently-delivered content (videos, articles, short posts) rather than relying on occasional mass emails. He explicitly warns against turning teachers into 'Swiss Army knives' who are expected to teach everything, arguing instead for role specialization paired with a schoolwide content library built over time.
points: Stuart's central claim: SEL should mostly happen as a byproduct of a loving, mastery-driven classroom rather than as explicit, separate instruction -- a 'reverse Mr. Rogers' approach where the subject is academic but the coincidental lesson is emotional and social.
He warns that turning classroom teachers into generalists responsible for explicit SEL instruction is a 'quixotic attempt' that pulls them away from developing deep subject-matter expertise.

For schoolwide SEL capacity-building, he recommends small, consistently-delivered content (a weekly video, article, or short post) over infrequent mass emails, because habit-formation beats one-off outreach.

He frames the content-library approach as having a long-term payoff: a team builds reusable resources (e.g., a video on conflict at home, a resource for perfectionism) that can be redeployed for years.
quotes: The presence of a consistent, loving adult is like a social/emotional petri dish.
The rule should be this: teaching all students toward mastery of your subject area. Because who else will do this in the child's life?

In your classroom, aim for the mirror version of Mr. Rogers' neighborhood. Yours is a place about English or science or health that coincidentally teaches students about other parts of being alive, too.
Folks outside of the classroom should get together and think up bold but simple solutions for building social-emotional capacity throughout the community over time.
You want to build a habit in as many folks as you can to look forward to your team's weekly or bi-weekly video/article/TikTok (shudder) about living better at home.
These two recommendations aren't going to work perfectly, but I think they'll work much better than what I see most of us doing right now.
